title: What is this? — ezafe, the link nobody writes
goal: Name the things around you, say who they belong to, and add adjectives — all through one linking sound that is the backbone of Persian.
bekal: link two words with ezafe to show possession and description
name colors and describe everyday things

dialogs.title: گفتگو — در اتاقِ کار
dialogs.intro: Maryam shows Budi her office at the language institute. Budi points at things and asks questions.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: این یک قلم است. قلمِ من.
lines.baca: in yek ghalam ast. ghalam-e man.
lines.literal: this one pen is. pen-of I.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: آن کتابِ فارسی است. کتابِ خوبی است.
lines.baca: ân ketâb-e fârsi ast. ketâb-e khubi ast.
lines.id: That's a Persian book. A good book.
lines.literal: that book-of Persian is. book-of good-a is.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: کیفِ قهوه‌ایِ من و عینکِ استاد.
lines.baca: kif-e ghahve'i-ye man va eynak-e ostâd.
lines.id: My brown bag and the lecturer's glasses.
lines.literal: bag-of brown-of I and glasses-of lecturer.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: ممنون. این پنجرهٔ بزرگ خیلی قشنگ است.
lines.baca: mamnun. in panjere-ye bozorg kheyli ghashang ast.
lines.id: Thank you. This big window is very lovely.
lines.literal: grateful-I. this window-of big very lovely is.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: بله. و آن گلدانِ آبی هم زیبا است.
lines.baca: bale. va ân goldân-e âbi ham zibâ ast.
lines.id: Yes. And that blue vase is pretty too.
lines.literal: yes. and that vase-of blue also pretty is.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.id: It's a gift from my mother.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.id: No, but she has good taste.

notes: **The spoken forms are much shorter:** این چیه؟ (*in chiye?*), اون چیه؟ (*un chiye?*), مالِ کیه؟ (*mâl-e kiye?*). This is what you'll hear in Iran; the چیست forms are what you'll mostly **read**.

**Ezafe at work: قلمِ من.** The -e sound stuck to the end of قلم links it to من. The order matters, and it's easy: **the thing owned comes first, the owner after** — قلمِ من is literally "pen-of me" — think *the pen of mine*, not *my pen*.

⚠️ **That ـِ mark is almost never printed.** Open any Iranian newspaper and you'll read قلم من with no mark at all — readers simply know to say *ghalam-e man*. This module prints it from unit 1 to unit 20 as a helper. Once you start reading outside it, the mark will vanish, and your job is to hear it in your head.

**Adjectives come AFTER the noun** — the reverse of English. کتابِ خوب = "good book" (literally "book-of good"), پنجرهٔ بزرگ = "big window", گلدانِ آبی = "blue vase". If you know French *vin rouge* or Spanish *casa blanca*, you already have the pattern.

⚠️ **But این and آن come BEFORE the noun.** این پنجرهٔ بزرگ = "this big window". Note that there is **no ezafe** between این and پنجره — demonstratives never take it. That's the one thing to remember from this unit beyond the main rule.
**The phrase سلیقهٔ خوبی دارد** uses the verb دارد ("has"), which we take apart in unit 4. For now, learn it whole: دارم ("I have"), دارید ("you have"), دارد ("he/she has").

grammars.title: Ezafe — the -e sound that links everything
body: This is the most important lesson in the whole module. Persian links a noun to its owner, its adjective, or a describing word with a single -e sound attached to the end of the **first** word. Its three uses:
after: **After a consonant**, ezafe is written as a small kasre ـِ and read *-e*: کتابِ من.
**After the vowels ا، و**, add ی: پایِ من (*pâ-ye man*), دانشجویِ خوب (*dâneshju-ye khub*).
**After a silent final ه**, add a small hamze on top: خانهٔ من (*khâne-ye man*), هدیهٔ مادر (*hediye-ye mâdar*). The spelling خانه‌ی من is also used and just as correct.
**After ی**, just say *-ye* with nothing added: صندلیِ من (*sandali-ye man*).
⚠️ **Ezafe is not a word and never stands alone.** It cannot be separated or stressed, and it adds no new stressed syllable. Say *ketâbe man* in one breath, not *ketâb ... e ... man*.

grammars.title: This and that — این و آن
after: **No ezafe after این and آن.** It's این کتاب, not اینِ کتاب. If there is an adjective, ezafe appears only between the noun and the adjective: این کتابِ بزرگ ("this big book").
When این or آن stands alone as the subject, it means "this"/"that" as a thing: این خوب است ("this is good"), آن مالِ من است ("that is mine").
Tehran speech: این → این (*in*), آن → **اون** (*un*), آنها → **اونا** (*unâ*), آنجا → **اونجا** (*unjâ*). This ân → un shift happens in many words; unit 14 deals with it.

blocks.text: Notice **دفتر** (*daftar*), "notebook" or "office": it goes back to Greek *diphthéra*, "parchment" — a cousin of English *diphtheria*. And **فرش** (*farsh*) is the word for every "Persian carpet" you have ever admired.

blocks.title: در has two very different meanings
items: As a noun, **در** = "door": درِ خانه (*dar-e khâne*, "the door of the house").
As a preposition, **در** = "in, at": در خانه (*dar khâne*, "at home"). The only difference is the ezafe. If the mark is there, you're safe; if it isn't — and in real life it isn't — context decides.

blocks.title: Three sentences for asking about anything
items: "What is this?" — این چیست؟ / این چیه؟
"Whose is it?" — مالِ کیست؟ / مالِ کیه؟
"What is it called in Persian?" — به فارسی چه می‌گویند؟ (*be fârsi che miguyand?*). This last one will be the tool you use most in Iran; learn it whole now — its structure will make sense in unit 9.
